title: Serving runtime hardware comparison: A100 / H100 / L40S (cloud SKUs + drivers)
body:
Summary:
This doc captures our initial hardware comparison runs focused on inference performance for our serving runtime. We compared NVIDIA A100, H100, and L40S-class cards across multiple cloud SKUs and driver/CUDA combinations to identify bottlenecks and quantify trade-offs for latency and throughput. The goal is pragmatic: recommend default SKUs and driver stacks for hosted and dedicated offerings, and note areas where runtime changes (kernel selection, batching, KV cache) could better exploit specific hardware.

High-level findings (TL;DR):
- H100 generally gives best single-request latency and higher throughput for larger models (>=13B) when using CUDA 12.x + cuDNN/FP8-friendly stacks, but requires newer drivers and tuning to realize gains.
- A100 (40GB) remains cost-effective for 7B–13B models on many workloads; shows lower variance on older CUDA stacks (11.8) and solid multi-instance throughput.
- L40S (L4/L40 class inference GPU) performs well for low-cost, high-concurrency workloads on smaller models (<=7B) and batched workloads, but runs out of memory for bigger models.
- Driver/CUDA matters: we observed up to ~20–30% throughput difference and 10–25% latency difference across driver+CUDA combos on the same hardware for identical runs.

Test matrix (summary):
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 40GB (p4d-like), NVIDIA H100 80GB (p5-like), NVIDIA L40S (inference class).
- Cloud SKUs tested: AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100 40GB), AWS p5.24xlarge (H100 80GB), GCP a2-highgpu (A100 variant), GCP hpc H100-ish SKUs, Azure NDv4/NCas_T4_v3 mapping for L40S-equivalent. (Notes below on exact SKU mapping per cloud provider.)
- Models: Llama2-7B-chat (13B-lite config disabled), Llama2-13B-chat, Mistral-7B (when smaller model comparison useful).
- Payloads: short-chat (prompt ~60 tokens, generate 128), medium summary (prompt ~200 tokens, generate 256), long generation (prompt ~500 tokens, generate 512).
- Runtime config: Redwood inference runtime v1.14 (baseline), batching disabled for p50 latency runs, batching enabled (target batch sizes 4/8/16) for throughput runs. KV cache warm vs cold tested.
- Driver/CUDA tested: NVIDIA driver 525 + CUDA 11.8, driver 535 + CUDA 12.0, driver 545 + CUDA 12.1 (where available). cuBLAS/cuDNN defaults for each stack.

Methodology
- Reproducible runner: automated benchmark harness (github PR linked) that provisions identical VM/software images, loads model weights from our S3/GCS cache, runs 5 warmup iterations then 50 measured iterations.
- Metrics captured: latency p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec (end-to-end), GPU utilization (nvidia-smi at 1s sample), GPU memory usage, host CPU load, power draw (where available), and failure/retry stats.
- Isolation: single-customer dedicated instance for single-GPU runs; contention-free tenancy. Multi-GPU runs tested with 1, 2, and 4-card partitions where supported.
- Notes: Results vary by microarchitecture, model size, sequence length distribution, and batching. The numbers below are representative medians across runs; see raw CSVs linked in Confluence.

Representative results (median of repeated runs)
- Llama2-7B-chat, short-chat (prompt 60 -> gen 128), batch=1 (cold KV):
  - A100 (CUDA11.8): p50=32ms, p95=78ms, tokens/sec=320
  - H100 (CUDA12.1): p50=24ms, p95=60ms, tokens/sec=420
  - L40S (CUDA12.0): p50=38ms, p95=92ms, tokens/sec=280

- Llama2-13B-chat, medium (prompt 200 -> gen 256), batch=1 (warm KV):
  - A100 (CUDA11.8): p50=120ms, p95=270ms, tokens/sec=165
  - H100 (CUDA12.1): p50=85ms, p95=180ms, tokens/sec=250
  - L40S (CUDA12.0): out-of-memory / swap or inconsistent (not recommended)

- Throughput run (Llama2-13B, batched gen 256, batch=8, warm KV):
  - A100 (CUDA11.8): aggregated tokens/sec=1,120,  GPU util ~78%
  - H100 (CUDA12.1): aggregated tokens/sec=1,820,  GPU util ~89%
  - L40S: N/A (memory limited)

Driver/CUDA impact (same A100 hardware, 13B workload):
- driver 525 / CUDA 11.8: tokens/sec=1,120 (baseline)
- driver 535 / CUDA 12.0: tokens/sec=1,280 (+14%); p95 improved ~12%
- driver 545 / CUDA 12.1: tokens/sec=1,380 (+23%); p95 improved ~20%
Interpretation: newer CUDA stacks expose kernel-level improvements and FP8/cuDNN enhancements for larger transformer matmuls. Gains are larger on H100 due to architectural support for newer instructions.

Profiling notes and bottlenecks observed
- Kernel hotspots: large GEMM (linear layers) and attention softmax remain the top hotspots. On H100 we observed more time in memory copies when using suboptimal kernel selection; tuning kernel selector reduced memcpy time by ~10%.
- NVLink / interconnect: multi-GPU runs sensitive to NCCL version and driver pairing; suboptimal NCCL caused ~15% lower multi-GPU throughput in initial runs.
- CPU-to-GPU transfer: for many short prompts, host-side batching queue and copy overhead contributes significantly to p95 latency. On A100 with older drivers the CPU copy loop was a noticeable fraction; switching to pinned buffers + async copies lowered p95 by ~8–12%.
- Kernel autoselect pitfalls: default kernel selector in the runtime chose suboptimal kernels for certain attention configs on H100 with CUDA12.1; adding a small kernel selector table for sequence lengths common in chat workloads fixed this.

Cost vs performance (high-level)
- H100 shows best latency and top-end throughput but at higher $/hour. For latency-sensitive, single-tenant offerings (enterprise dedicated) H100 is the recommended default for large models (>=13B).
- A100 balances cost and performance for mid-size models and multi-tenant hosted API where throughput per dollar matters. For 7B models A100 is typically the best cost/latency sweet spot.
- L40S is attractive for cheap inference of small models and for scaling high concurrency when model fits memory limits. Not suitable for 13B+ unless model sharding / offloading implemented.

Immediate recommendations
1) Hosted API defaults: use A100-family SKUs for general hosted API tiers; offer H100 as a premium low-latency tier for large-model-heavy customers. For small-model-only workloads provide L40S-backed SKU to reduce unit cost.
2) Driver stacks: standardize images on CUDA 12.1 + NVIDIA driver >=545 for H100 fleets; keep a tested A100 image on CUDA 11.8 for stability, but validate CUDA12.x for A100 host images (we saw positive gains). Maintain clear mapping matrix in deployment docs.
3) Runtime tuning: invest in kernel selector improvements (sequence-length-aware heuristics), ensure pinned buffers + async memcpy path for short-prompt p95 improvements, and test NCCL versions as part of multi-GPU presubmit.
4) Dedicated offering: for reserved capacity contracts targeting large models, recommend H100-backed instance types with validated driver/CUDA. Include optional model-quantization recommendations (8-bit/FP8) to further reduce memory pressure.

Open questions / next steps
- Run expanded matrix including Llama2-70B on 4xH100 to measure sharded performance and interconnect/NVLink impacts.
- Test FP8 / H100-specific kernels with quantized weights to evaluate memory and latency trade-offs.
- Add power/cost profiling to derive tokens-per-watt and tokens-per-dollar numbers for realistic cost math across cloud SKUs.
- Validate results across multiple cloud regions and exact SKU variants (p5 vs p5d on AWS, GCP H100 variants) to catch driver/firmware differences.

Appendix: quick reproducibility notes
- Benchmark harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/benchmarks/hw-comparison (see PR linked above).
- AMI/container images used: redwood/base-infer:cuda11.8-driver525 (A100 baseline), redwood/base-infer:cuda12.1-driver545 (H100 baseline).
- Commands: ./bench/run_benchmark.sh --model llama2-13b --device gpu --batch 1 --cuda 12.1 --iterations 50 --warmup 5  (full runner flags in repo)

Notes / caveats
- These are early runs; numbers are sensitive to exact model builds (tokenizer differences and operator fuse changes). Consider this a directional guide for architecture and procurement decisions rather than a billing SLA.
- OOM behavior on L40S indicates we should include memory-profiling shim in runtime to early-detect and gracefully fallback to smaller model variants.

If you want, I can:
- Push raw CSV outputs and plotting scripts to Confluence (linked)
- Spin a follow-up run focusing on H100 FP8 quantization (need 2–3 days of runs)

Authors: Jordan Patel (author), Avery Chen, Priya Singh, Marco Alvarez.
